headline: High-risk default interaction: open-webui can ingest files and external tools while agentic-flow can run shell/MCP and modify git, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b exposes files, mounted volumes, browsers, and MCP/OpenAPI tools. That creates a default bridge where content from B can be fed into A’s tool-use path and vice versa. Because A also runs shell and subprocesses, injected instructions can propagate into actions. The shared MCP surface makes this more than manual copy-paste.
conditions: IF agent_b loads untrusted documents or web content into prompts
IF agent_a consumes MCP/stdin content as instructions without provenance checks
IF both agents are connected through the same MCP server or shared workspace
mitigations: Disable shared MCP endpoints between the agents
Route B’s file inputs through a read-only staging folder
Add a provenance banner to all B-to-A content
Require manual approval before A executes shell or git actions
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b touches files, mounted volumes, API keys, and persistent memory, while agent_a can execute shell, modify git state, and use network egress plus GitHub/MCP. If they share a workspace or credentials, A can exfiltrate B’s sensitive data through allowed outbound channels. The profiles do not show isolation strong enough to rule this out, so uncertainty escalates.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a filesystem, mounted volume, or credentials
IF B stores API keys or documents in a location A can read
IF A is allowed to send data to GitHub or other allowlisted network destinations
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different volumes
Rotate any shared API keys before co-running
Restrict A’s outbound allowlist to non-sensitive endpoints
Mount B’s data read-only for A
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can modify git state and spawn subprocesses, and agent_b supports persistent shared sessions with Redis-backed shared state across instances. If both operate on the same repository or mutable workspace, concurrent writes can race and corrupt state. The profiles do not show locking or coordination primitives, so the conflict pathway exists in common deployments.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git repository or working directory
IF agent_b instances share Redis-backed session state while A edits the same artifacts
IF no external lock or transaction layer is present
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Pause one agent during git commits
Use a lock file around shared mutable resources
Review diffs before merge or push
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_b can render or act on prompts, documents, and artifacts, while agent_a can generate outputs after shell/MCP-driven analysis. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, A’s mistakes can cascade into browser actions, tool calls, or persisted artifacts. No verification step is documented, so the safer assumption is that the handoff is untrusted and dangerous by default.
conditions: IF B uses A’s output as input to tools, browsers, or saved artifacts
IF A produces facts, commands, or citations that B does not verify
IF downstream actions are enabled in B’s toolchain
mitigations: Insert a human review step between A and B
Require B to verify A’s claims against source documents
Disable auto-execution of tool outputs from A
Log and diff A-to-B handoffs for review
requires-engineering: implement structured validation of A outputs

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b explicitly handles API keys, documents, notes, calendar events, and persistent memory, while agent_a handles task prompts, repository metadata, and Ed25519 signatures. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or certification boundaries, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because uncertainty escalates and B’s data classes are broader, medium is the prudent choice.
conditions: IF regulated data such as customer documents or calendar events are stored in B
IF A processes signatures or repository metadata under a different retention policy
IF either agent is deployed in a jurisdiction with residency or DPA constraints
mitigations: Classify data before sending it to either agent
Keep regulated data out of B unless policy is confirmed
Document retention and deletion settings for both agents
Restrict secrets handling to a single approved agent
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
